278.t: Of uncertain origin. Beekes compares χήρα (khḗra, “widow”), assuming common derivation from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave behind”), with original meaning "unoccupied (left-behind) space".

224.t: From Proto-Hellenic *ágō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti (“to be driving”), from the root *h₂eǵ- (“to drive”). Cognate with Latin agō (“to act; to do; to drive”), Sanskrit अजति (ájati, “he drives”).

208.t: Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀐𐀫 (a-ke-ro), with further origin uncertain.

280.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pénkʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. Cognates include Sanskrit पञ्च (páñca), Latin quīnque, Old Armenian հինգ (hing) and Old English fīf (English five).

211.t: Hellenized form of Semitic proper name roughly equivalent to Ἰησοῦ (Ĭēsoû) + -ς (-s); Hellenic case suffixes added to an approximated Greek literal phonetic rendering of Aramaic יֵשׁוּע (yēšū́ʿ, “Jesus”) and Biblical Hebrew יֵשׁוּעַ (yēšū́aʿ, “Jesus” or…

262.t: From Biblical Hebrew יוֹסֵף (Yōsēp̄). Doublet of Ἰώσηπος (Iṓsēpos).

200.t: Probably formed innovatively from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to fill”) + -ος (-os). Compare the relationship between πλῆθος (plêthos) ~ πλήθω (plḗthō) ~ πέπληθα (péplētha) and βριθύς (brithús, “heavy”) ~ βρίθω (bríthō) ~ βέβριθα (bébritha).

270.t: From ἄρχω (árkhō, “to begin, to be first in order”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).

214.t: A Proto-Indo-European etymology as a compound *m̥ǵh₂-peh₂- (from *méǵh₂- (“great”) + *peh₂- (“to protect”), literally “[provide] great protection”) was proposed by Pinault in 1991; see ἀγα- (ăgă-, “way too”) for the first component.

235.t: From Proto-Hellenic *holwos, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂wós, from *solh₂- (“whole”). Cognates include Sanskrit सर्व (sárva), Avestan 𐬵𐬀𐬎𐬭𐬬𐬀 (haurva), Latin salvus, sollus.

253.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hə́teros, from Proto-Indo-European *sḿ̥teros, from the zero grade of the root *sem- (“one", from which also comes Ancient Greek εἷς (heîs), "one”) + *-teros (contrastive suffix, from which also comes Ancient Greek -τερος (-teros)).

285.t: From Ἰουδά (Ioudá) + -ιος (-ios), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yəhūḏā(h), “Judah”).

287.t: From Proto-Hellenic *súrks, *swə́rks, originally denoting "a piece of meat", from Proto-Indo-European *turḱ-s, a zero-grade s-stem nominal from the root *twerḱ- (“to cut”).

282.t: From Proto-Hellenic *deksiwós, from Proto-Indo-European *deḱs-. Cognate with Sanskrit दक्षिण (dákṣiṇa) and Latin dexter.

284.t: From συνάγω (sunágō, “to gather together”) + -ή (-ḗ), from σύν (sún, “with, together”) + ἄγω (ágō, “to lead”).

252.t: From Proto-Hellenic *agrós, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵros. Cognates include Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀒𐀫 (a-ko-ro), Latin ager, Sanskrit अज्र (ájra) and Old English æcer (English acre).

212.t: From Proto-Indo-European *peh₃- (“to drink”). Cognates include Sanskrit पिब॑ति (píbati), Latin pōtō and bibō, and Albanian pi.

213.t: According to Beekes and Chantraine, probably from Pre-Greek. Older theories link the word to εἴρω (eírō, “to fasten together”) or εἴρω (eírō, “to speak, say”); compare ῥήτρα (rhḗtra, “verbal agreement, treaty”).

243.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hekətón, see there for more. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

222.t: From γέννα (génna) + -άω (-ắō), poetic form of γένος (génos, “offspring”). Causal counterpart of γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be born, to become”).

286.t: Formally it would be from Proto-Hellenic *genehā́, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵenh₁eseh₂, feminine derivation from *ǵénh₁os (whence γένος (génos)), from *ǵenh₁-. Compare εἶδος (eîdos) - ἰδέα (idéa).

238.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pró, from Proto-Indo-European *pró, *pro- (see *per-). Cognates include Latin pro, Sanskrit प्र- (prá-), Proto-Celtic *ɸro and Proto-Germanic *fram (English from).

249.t: Uncertain, though most theories imply a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out; to fly”) by relating the term to reflexes as such: * πίπτω (pī́ptō, “to fall”), thus a "waterfall" > "river that sweeps things away", * πετάννυμι…

266.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kalwós, probably from Proto-Indo-European *kal-wo-s, formed from *kal- (“beautiful”). Cognate with Sanskrit कल्य (kalya), Sanskrit क॒ल्याण॑ (kalyā́ṇa), Albanian kolmë.

264.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰéugō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg- (“to flee”). Related to φυγή (phugḗ, verbal noun) and Latin fugiō.

283.t: Together with Mycenaean Greek 𐀅𐀗 (da-mo), traceable back to Proto-Hellenic *dā́mos, inherited from Proto-Indo-European *déh₂mos (“part, division”), from *deh₂- (“to share, divide”) + *-mos.

296.t: From Proto-Hellenic *méns (“month”), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”), probably from *meh₁- (“to measure”). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀕𐀜 (me-no), Latin mēnsis (“month”), and English moon, month.

277.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tʰurā, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer- (“door”). Cognates include Sanskrit द्वार् (dvā́r), Latin foris, Old Armenian դուռն (duṙn) and Old English duru and dor (English door) and Russian дверь (dverʹ).

247.t: From ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + σέβομαι (sébomai, “I feel awe”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjective suffix).

219.t: From Proto-Hellenic *nuks, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”). Cognates include Latin nox, Sanskrit नक्त् (nákt), Old Church Slavonic нощь (noštĭ), Albanian natë and Old English niht (whence English night).

261.t: From Proto-Hellenic *wóinos (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀺𐀜 (wo-no)), from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁ō; related to English wine, Latin vīnum, Old Armenian գինի (gini) etc.; according to the Oxford Latin Dictionary, "all probably from a common Mediterranean…

218.t: From Proto-Hellenic *spérmə, from Proto-Indo-European *spérmn̥, which consists of Proto-Indo-European *sper- + *-mn̥. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀟𐀗 (pe-mo).

263.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kríňňō, from Proto-Indo-European *kri-n-yé-ti, from *krey- (“to sift, separate”). Cognates include English rinse, Latin cernō (“to separate, discern”), and Welsh gogrynu.

227.t: According to Beekes (2010), “the relation between οὖν and ὦν is unclear. Unconvincing explanations in Brugmann-Thumb 1913: 633 and in Schwyzer 1950: 586f.

209.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *-kʷe (“and”). Cognates include Mycenaean Greek 𐀤 (qe), Phrygian κε (ke), Sanskrit च (ca), and Latin -que.

271.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dews-? Proto-Indo-European *-teros Ancient Greek -τερος (-teros) Ancient Greek δεύτερος Uncertain.

279.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ Proto-Indo-European *dwi- Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥ Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)wídḱm̥ti Proto-Hellenic *ewī́kəti Ancient Greek εἴκοσι From Proto-Hellenic *ewī́kəti, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)wídḱm̥ti (“twenty”).

228.t: From οὐδέ (oudé, “and not, not even”) + εἷς (heîs, “one”). Sometimes reanalysed as οὐ (ou, “no, not”) + δείς (deís, “no one, nothing”), as a result of the later variant, οὐθείς (outheís).

230.t: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mneh₂- (“to remind”), which is generally thought to be a root extension of *men- (“to remember, think”), with inchoative suffix -σκω (-skō).

288.t: From ἄδικος (ắdĭkos, “unjust, wrong”) + -ία (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix).

246.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pā́kʰus, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂ǵʰús. Cognates include Sanskrit बाहु (bāhu, “arm”), Old Persian 𐎲𐎠𐏀𐎢 (b-a-z-u /⁠bāzu⁠/) (Persian بازو (bâzu)), and Old English bōg (English bough).

237.t: Although there are no known cognates outside of Greek, Beekes nonetheless reconstructs a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mert- (“to miss, fail”) as the ancestor of this word, arguing that the root structure "looks perfectly IE." See νημερτής (nēmertḗs) for a…

234.t: From ἀπο- (apo-, “from, away from”) + κρίνω (krínō, “to separate, distinguish, judge”).

250.t: Proto-Hellenic *tókʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *to- + *-kʷe. Compare ὅτε (hóte), πότε (póte).

272.t: From an original *τῖβωτός (*tîbōtós), from Aramaic תֵּיבוֹתָא (tēḇōṯā), from a merger of Egyptian DbA-b-t:pr (ḏbꜣt, “sarcophagus, coffin”) and d-b-t:xt (dbt, “chest, box”), as also synonymous Arabic تَابُوت (tābūt) and Hebrew תֵּבָה (tēḇā́).

240.t: From relative ὅς (hós) (or from its stem) + indefinite πως (pōs). Compare ὡς (hōs).

205.t: From Proto-Hellenic *t͏̌āmeron, for earlier *ki-hāmeron, with the first component from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe (“this, here”). By surface analysis, a univerbation of κί- (kí-) + ἡμέρα (hēmérā, “day”).

260.t: A perfective verb of uncertain origin, but seems to be related to the present-meaning ἵκω (híkō, “to come”), and thus from Proto-Indo-European *seyk- (“to reach for”), though the aspectual difference and phonetics are difficult to resolve.

289.t: From ὕψι (hŭ́psi, “high”), ὕψος (hŭ́psos, “height; summit”) + -λός (-lós). Compare Proto-Celtic *ouxselos, whence Old Irish úasal, Welsh uchel and the first part of Gaulish Uxellodunum.

292.t: Adverbial use of declination of πλησίος (plēsíos).

248.t: Borrowed from Thracian, ultimately possibly from Proto-Indo-European *Hrewp- (“to break”), likely closely related to Albanian rrufé (“lightning”).

256.t: According to Beekes, related to Old Armenian մոզի (mozi, “calf”) and maybe from a Proto-Indo-European *mosǵʰ-o- (“young of an animal; young shoot”).

202.t: From χρυσός (khrūsós, “gold”) + -ιον (-ĭon, “diminutive suffix”). See χρυσός (khrusós) for further etymology.
